A 36-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of low-grade fever and severe stabbing headaches. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Neurological examination was unremarkable except for marked meningeal signs. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the head revealed no abnormalities. CSF analysis demonstrated inflammatory findings with lymphocytic pleocytosis (183 cells/μL; 97.8% lymphocytes) and elevated protein concentration (83.3 mg/dL). CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing did not identify an infectious etiology. Serological testing for tick-borne infections, including Borrelia burgdorferi, was negative. Based on the clinical presentation and initial laboratory findings, the patient was initially diagnosed with lymphocytic meningitis syndrome. She received intravenous dexamethasone (Dexaven) for 9 days, starting at 8 mg/day for 2 days, followed by 12 mg/day for 3 days, then tapered to 8 mg/day for 3 days and 4 mg/day on the final day, together with symptomatic treatment. A follow-up lumbar puncture showed partial improvement, with a WBC count of 130 cells/μL and protein concentration of 46.1 mg/dL. After 12 days of hospitalization, she was discharged in good condition on 11 March 2026. message.content: no abnormalities. However, given the persistent and worsening symptoms, a brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with gadolinium contrast was obtained, which revealed a 2.3 × 1.8 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe with surrounding vasogenic edema and mild mass effect on the adjacent lateral ventricle. No other lesions were identified. The patient was readmitted, and a repeat lumbar puncture was performed. CSF analysis now showed a WBC count of 210 cells/μL with 94% lymphocytes, protein of 98.6 mg/dL, and glucose of 38 mg/dL. CSF cytology revealed atypical large lymphoid cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios. Flow cytometry of the CSF demonstrated a monoclonal B-cell population expressing CD19, CD20, and CD22 with loss of CD5 and CD10. A stereotactic brain biopsy was performed under general anesthesia. Histopathological examination revealed a diffuse infiltration of atypical large lymphoid cells with centroblastic morphology. Immunohistochemistry confirmed positivity for CD20, PAX5, and MUM1, with a Ki-67 proliferation index of approximately 80%. The cells were negative for CD3, CD5, and CD10. The final diagnosis was primary central nervous system diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PCNS-DLBCL). The patient was referred to a multidisciplinary tumor board, and treatment with high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy was initiated. After four cycles of induction therapy, a follow-up brain MRI demonstrated a significant reduction in the size of the lesion with resolution of the surrounding edema. The patient's headache and photophobia improved substantially. She was discharged with plans for consolidation therapy and close radiological surveillance. This case underscores the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for PCNS-DLBCL in patients with apparent aseptic meningitis who fail to respond adequately to empiric treatment, and highlights the critical role of CSF cytology, flow cytometry, and tissue biopsy in establishing the definitive diagnosis.
